To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
fathers experience childhood cancer differently from mothers because they are men and because of the gendered organization and expectations of the family, health care, and employment systems.

fathers of children with leukemia or other forms of cancer experience stress and distress, and their experience is shaped by the gender roles they are socialized to play, the gendered structure of their support systems, and the gender roles and styles of the health care professionals who care for their children.
fathers of children with childhood cancer are affected by gender roles, gender styles, and the gender organization of social support, employment, and the health care system.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the gender roles of fathers and the gender styles of mothers and fathers in the context of a child’s life-threatening illness.
how fathers and mothers cope with the stress of childhood cancer.
the gendered nature of parental experiences in the context of childhood cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the experiences of fathers can be understood as a complex interaction among their own gender identities and gender roles, their gendered organization of social support systems, and the gender roles and styles of their wives, children, and other family members.
the gender role of the father has been changing over the years, and it is not as important to be the sole provider as it was in the past.
the gender roles and styles of fathers of children diagnosed with cancer are affected in many ways.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
gender roles and styles influence the experience of fathers in crisis.
fathers of children with a life-threatening illness are not just “moms in drag” but are men with unique experiences that are shaped by their gender roles and gendered social structures.
gender roles and styles in crisis are integrative.
The main takeaway from our work is that
gender roles and/or styles play an important role in the experiences of parents of children with cancer.
the experiences of fathers can be viewed through the lens of masculinity, gender roles, gendered social institutions, and the gendering of social support.
the gender roles of fathers and mothers are not fixed, but are dynamic.
